name: Independent on Sunday cryptic crossword No 1,468

clue.text: The royal couple have loads of affairs

blocks.note: Prince Philip and Elizabeth Regina, the late Queen, read as a pair

explanation.surface: A gossip column claims the King and Queen are both carrying on behind each other's backs.
explanation.walkthrough: PHIL AND ER: Prince Philip plus ER, the Latin initials of Queen Elizabeth (Elizabeth Regina).
explanation.definitionFit: To philander is a verb for a man chasing many casual romances, which matches carrying on numerous flings.

clue.text: Request certain to give sexual gratification

blocks.note: a plea is an earnest request
sure means certain

explanation.surface: Someone is told that asking nicely is a guaranteed route to satisfaction in bed.
explanation.definitionFit: Pleasure is a general word for enjoyment, often used specifically of physical or erotic delight.

clue.text: Opening Republican's interested in securing

indicators.note: securing something means holding it fast within, so one piece is gripped inside the other

blocks.note: to be into something is to be keen on it
standard abbreviation for Republican

explanation.surface: A Republican politician shows interest in landing an opening deal.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's is short for 'is': the R is held inside INTO.
explanation.definitionFit: An intro is the opening section of a song, speech or book, its brief introductory passage.

clue.text: A good beer and ale drunk could be thus

definitions.text: A good beer and ale drunk could be thus

indicators.note: drink that has been drunk is jumbled up inside you, so the two drinks' letters are mixed

blocks.note: taken as written
G is the usual abbreviation for good
taken as written, to be mixed
taken as written, to be mixed

explanation.surface: A pleasant pint or two leaves the drinker in a mellow mood.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is also the definition: someone who has drunk a good beer and some ale may well be in an amiable mood.
explanation.definitionFit: Agreeable describes a pleasant, amiable state, which is how a couple of nice drinks often leave someone.

clue.text: Run lewdly about, but I won't emit any gas!

indicators.note: running about means moving all over the place, so these letters are scattered into a new order

blocks.note: R is the cricket abbreviation for run
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone cavorts indecently but promises not to break wind.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'gas' is natural gas from a borehole, not flatulence; a dry well is one drilled that yields nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: A dry well is a borehole that produces no oil or natural gas, so it speaks the definition's line.

clue.text: Queen pot-bellied on removing top? Sexy!

indicators.note: taking off the top of a down word means dropping its first letter

blocks.note: R for Regina, Latin for queen
a paunch is a pot belly

explanation.surface: A tubby queen strips off her top, and someone finds this arousing.
explanation.definitionFit: Raunchy means earthy and sexually explicit, a close synonym for sexy in a coarse sense.

clue.text: I'm in Lourdes, but I ain't seen The Lord!

indicators.note: something not seen is missing, so this letter is taken away

blocks.note: French for 'I am', Lourdes being in France
the letter to be dropped

explanation.surface: A pilgrim at the shrine of Lourdes complains of no divine vision.
explanation.walkthrough: JE SUIS is French for 'I am'; remove its I to leave the name.
explanation.definitionFit: Christians address and refer to Christ as the Lord, so the name is a direct equivalent.

clue.text: What one might say to jerk that's tipsy?

blocks.note: to jog is to jolt or nudge abruptly
to be a bit on is British slang for being slightly drunk

explanation.surface: What would you tell an annoying drunk idiot?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jog on!' is British slang for 'go away!', exactly what you might tell a drunken jerk, so the surface reading supports the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Jog on is a dismissive British exclamation telling someone to clear off, an utterance one might say.

clue.text: Gloomy function opened by a performer

indicators.note: a thing opened up has something pushed into its middle

blocks.note: sine is a trigonometric function
a turn is a variety act or performer

explanation.surface: A dull party gets started by an entertainer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Function' suggests a party, but it is the maths function, split S...INE.
explanation.definitionFit: Saturnine describes a sullen, morose temperament, traditionally linked to the planet Saturn's dark influence.

clue.text: Half-pint of small prawns by the looks of them?

definitions.note: plural in the clue; the answer names one of them

blocks.note: first meaning: a very small person
second meaning: a small edible crustacean

explanation.surface: A little person resembles a tiny seafood creature.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Half-pint' sounds like beer, but it is slang for a short person, who is nicknamed after the tiny crustacean.
explanation.definitionFit: A shrimp is both a tiny edible crustacean and an insulting nickname for an undersized person.

clue.text: Submit landlord should be relieved of capital

indicators.note: losing the capital means losing the first letter, the head of the word

blocks.note: one who rents out property

explanation.surface: A tenant demands that a landlord be stripped of his money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Capital' looks like money, but it means the first letter of the word.
explanation.definitionFit: To enter something, such as a competition piece or a plea, is to submit it formally.

clue.text: Tiddler? Get yours operated on around November

indicators.note: something operated on has been cut open and worked over, so these letters are rearranged
the rearranged letters go round the other piece, enclosing it

blocks.note: taken as written
N is November in the NATO alphabet

explanation.surface: A doctor tells someone their tonsils will come out in November, while calling them a little one.
explanation.definitionFit: A tiddler is British slang for a small child, and a youngster is a young person.

clue.text: What I think Hoskins-haters might do? Good grief!

definitions.text: What I think Hoskins-haters might do

blocks.clueFragment: What I think Hoskins-haters might do
blocks.note: first meaning: the setter imagines critics pelting him with rocks
second meaning: a British exclamation of surprise or exasperation

explanation.surface: The setter Hoskins wonders what people who hate his puzzles would do to him, and sighs.
explanation.walkthrough: Hoskins is this puzzle's setter, so 'me' is him. 'Stone me!' is a British exclamation, like 'good grief!'.
explanation.definitionFit: Both phrases are mild exclamations of astonishment, and literally the setter asks to be pelted with rocks.

clue.text: Body part beset by some indecent rumblings

indicators.note: surrounded by part of the following words, so the answer sits inside them

blocks.note: letters running across the two words

explanation.surface: Someone's insides are troubled by rude gurgling noises.
explanation.definitionFit: The centrum is the main solid body of a vertebra, an anatomical part of the spine.

clue.text: All beer needs to be reordered? Call again!

indicators.note: placing a fresh order changes the sequence, so these letters go in a different order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: The pub has run dry and the landlord must phone the brewery again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reordered' and 'Call again' both suggest a bar restocking; the call is a naming, not a phone call.
explanation.definitionFit: To relabel something is to give it a new name, that is to call it something different once more.

clue.text: City passes on board member? He's a Lothario

blocks.note: Los Angeles
to pass on or away is to die
a piece on a chess or draughts board is a man

explanation.surface: A city hands something over to a member of the company board, who turns out to be a womaniser.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Board member' suggests a director; it is a playing piece on a board.
explanation.definitionFit: Lothario, a seducer in an old play, is a byword for a womaniser, as is a man who charms women.

clue.text: Jamaican criminal that's tailing detectives

indicators.note: to tail is to follow behind, so this piece comes after the other

blocks.note: the Yard is Scotland Yard, London's police headquarters, so its detectives
i.e. abbreviates id est, 'that is'

explanation.surface: A gangster from Jamaica is being followed by police officers.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface has the detectives tailing the criminal; the wordplay reverses this, with 'that's' following the detectives.
explanation.definitionFit: Yardie is the term for a member of a Jamaican organised-crime gang, especially one operating in Britain.

clue.text: Vacuous Etonian tucking into relaxing bitter

indicators.note: something vacuous is empty, so the inside of the word is cleared out
to tuck into something is to get inside it

blocks.note: restful means calming and relaxing
just the first and last letters remain

explanation.surface: An empty-headed public schoolboy settles down to enjoy a pint of bitter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bitter' sounds like the beer the Etonian is drinking, but it is the adjective defining the answer. Eton is an elite English boarding school.
explanation.definitionFit: Resentful means full of bitter indignation at being treated unfairly, an aggrieved and sour feeling.

clue.text: Fulfilled a large desire after some fiddling

indicators.note: fiddling with something means tinkering about with it, so these letters are mixed

blocks.note: taken as written
L is the clothing-size abbreviation for large
taken as written

explanation.surface: A great longing is satisfied after a bit of illicit fumbling.
explanation.definitionFit: To realise an ambition or hope is to achieve it, so a realised wish has been accomplished.

clue.text: Commercial area by deserted green in Paris

blocks.note: standard abbreviation for area
D is a recognised abbreviation for deserted
the French word for green

explanation.surface: A shopping district sits beside an empty park in the French capital.
explanation.definitionFit: A commercial, as a noun, is a broadcast advertisement, the same thing as a promotional plug.

clue.text: Constant barrage? Time enlisted men split

blocks.note: T is the abbreviation for time
other ranks, soldiers who are not officers
rent is the past tense of rend, to tear apart

explanation.surface: Under relentless shelling, the soldiers decide it is time to scatter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Constant barrage' suggests artillery, but it means an unceasing stream, as of abuse or questions.
explanation.definitionFit: A torrent is a violent rushing flow, used figuratively for an overwhelming outpouring of words.

clue.text: View posterior of old boy - that's indecent

indicators.note: posterior means coming behind, so this piece follows the other

blocks.note: OB is short for old boy, a former pupil
a scene is a view or vista

explanation.surface: Catching sight of an old man's bare bottom is described as lewd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Posterior' looks like a backside, but it is a placement word: the view comes behind.
explanation.definitionFit: Obscene means offensive to accepted standards of decency, especially in a sexual way.

clue.text: Very busy earl wears old thong in error

indicators.note: something worn is put on around the body, so the other letters enclose this one
a mistaken arrangement puts the letters wrongly, so they are reshuffled

blocks.note: O is the abbreviation for old
taken as written
E is the abbreviation for earl

explanation.surface: A frantic aristocrat accidentally puts on a worn-out G-string.
explanation.definitionFit: Being on the go means constantly active and moving about, with no time to rest.

clue.text: Distance unit is behind charging policeman

indicators.note: charging a vessel means filling it, so one piece is loaded into the other

blocks.note: a police constable
British slang for the backside

explanation.surface: Someone lags behind a police officer who is rushing forward or making an arrest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Behind' looks like a position word but is the noun for a bottom.
explanation.definitionFit: A parsec is an astronomical measure of length, about 3.26 light years.

clue.text: Superior needs bit of acid on head? I'll help!

definitions.note: the answer is the noun for someone who says this

indicators.note: a small bit of the word means only its opening letter is used
placed at the head, this piece goes at the start of the other

blocks.note: the first letter alone is used
better means superior

explanation.surface: A boss is suffering an acid burn to the scalp and someone rushes to assist.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the helper's own words: an abetter is the one who says 'I'll help!'.
explanation.definitionFit: An abetter is a person who assists or encourages another, typically in wrongdoing.

clue.text: Viz character who's foolish about love

indicators.note: this word placed around the other means it surrounds it

blocks.note: a twit is a silly person
love is zero in tennis, shaped like O

explanation.surface: A cartoon character from Viz magazine is a fool about romance.
explanation.walkthrough: Viz is a rude British comic, but here it is the abbreviation meaning 'namely'.
explanation.definitionFit: Viz is short for videlicet, Latin for namely, which the phrase to wit also means.

clue.text: Youngster? Bit short to be a bit of a climber

indicators.note: cut short means the word loses its final letter

blocks.note: read as a ten-year-old child
a drill bit, the boring tool's cutting part

explanation.surface: A child, slightly undersized, is set to become a little mountaineer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Youngster' for TEN, a child of ten, is a loose stretch; 'Bit' stands for the drill in which it fits.
explanation.definitionFit: A tendril is the slender coiling shoot by which a climbing plant clings, so it is part of one.

clue.text: Dangerous to be high-spirited? F*** off!

indicators.note: this letter being taken off means it is removed from the word

blocks.note: frisky means lively and playful
the letter to be dropped, its asterisks covering the swear word

explanation.surface: Someone is warned, with a censored expletive, that being too boisterous is hazardous.
explanation.walkthrough: The asterisked swear word is really just the letter F; take it off the word for high-spirited.
explanation.definitionFit: Risky means involving the chance of harm or loss, so close to dangerous.

clue.text: She wore me out (in an unnamed spot)

indicators.note: worn out means used up and broken, so these letters are knocked into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A man confesses his partner exhausted him, coyly declining to say where.
explanation.walkthrough: The bracketed coy aside is the definition, not a stage direction.
explanation.definitionFit: Somewhere is an adverb for at a place not specified or known, an unidentified location.

clue.text: Dukes right to pull out of top degrees

indicators.note: pulling a letter out of a word removes it from inside

blocks.note: a first is the highest class of British university degree
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: Aristocrats are entitled to withdraw from top-class university qualifications.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dukes' looks like noblemen but is slang for fists, as in 'put up your dukes'.
explanation.definitionFit: Dukes is old slang for the hands clenched for fighting, from rhyming slang Duke of Yorks for forks.

clue.text: Belt up and do loads of drugs? (but not E)

indicators.note: excluding something means leaving that letter out

blocks.note: to cane it is British slang for indulging to excess, drugs included
the letter to be dropped; E is also slang for ecstasy

explanation.surface: Someone is told to shut up and go on a drug binge, though steering clear of ecstasy.
explanation.walkthrough: Belt up is British for 'shut up', not fastening a seatbelt; E is both ecstasy and the letter removed.
explanation.definitionFit: Can it and belt up are both rude slang commands telling someone to stop talking.

clue.text: One living under bridge regarded as very drunk

blocks.note: as in the fairy tale of the three billy goats
to eye is to look at

explanation.surface: A rough sleeper under a bridge is assumed to be paralytic.
explanation.walkthrough: Trolleyed is British slang for heavily intoxicated.
explanation.definitionFit: Trolleyed is informal British slang for being extremely intoxicated, legless from alcohol.
